clue.text: Girl picked up small badger

indicators.note: In a down clue, picking something up lifts it, so the name is read from the bottom up

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A girl scoops up a little badger, the animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' looks like the animal from the surface, but here it is the verb: to pester someone relentlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean pestering someone with repeated, persistent demands.

clue.text: Surprise when mate gets round National Insurance

indicators.note: to get round something is to circle it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: as = when, as in 'as I left'
tosh is a British slang form of address for a man, like 'mate'
NI = National Insurance, the UK payroll contribution

explanation.surface: Someone is taken aback when a friend manages to dodge their National Insurance payments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tosh' as a word for a mate is dated British slang ('Oi, tosh!'); National Insurance is the UK's social-security deduction from wages.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean catching someone off guard with something unexpected.

clue.text: Smart to trap opponent in bridge

indicators.note: a trap closes on its catch, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: an anti is someone opposed to something

explanation.surface: Advice for card players: the smart move is to catch an opponent out during a game of bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' reads as the card game where you have opponents, but it is the structure; ANTI is an opponent as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A type of bridge built from beams fixed at one end only, projecting out to carry the span.

clue.text: Blue joke appearing first warrants severe action

indicators.note: this says the word just before it is placed at the front, ahead of the other piece

blocks.note: a crack is a wisecrack, a joke

explanation.surface: A dirty joke told up front gets the censors to clamp down hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue joke' reads as one phrase, a smutty gag, but the two words work separately: blue for sad, joke for crack.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the noun names a sudden, strict official campaign to stamp out wrongdoing.

clue.text: Spiritual leader absorbed in anima mundi

indicators.note: something absorbed is soaked up inside, so the letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the break between the two Latin words, from the end of the first into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A spiritual leader is lost in contemplation of the anima mundi.
explanation.walkthrough: The anima mundi is the 'world soul' of Plato and later mystics, which gives the surface its spiritual air.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the man who leads prayers in a mosque is a Muslim religious figure.

clue.text: One dozing having been given a smoke?

definitions.note: describes a kipper (a smoked herring) rather than meaning the word

blocks.note: one who kips, British slang for sleeps
a herring that has been split, salted and smoked

explanation.walkthrough: To kip is British slang for to sleep, so one who kips fits the first half; the question mark flags the playful second half, a smoked herring.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is a jokey coinage from the slang verb for sleep; the second describes the cured fish, with the question mark owning up to the stretch.

clue.text: Answer cry for help to protect finest building material

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding and shielding it, so one piece wraps the other

explanation.surface: A call for help goes out to save the best building material.
explanation.walkthrough: The irony is that this mineral is now the building material people cry for help to have removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibrous fireproof mineral once widely used in roofing, insulation and cement sheets for construction.

clue.text: Where Cranmer for example died is in dispute

definitions.note: a place phrase: at the stake

blocks.note: Cranmer was burnt at the stake
an idiom for something being risked or contested

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, was burnt in 1556 under Mary I; 'for example' says he is one of many martyrs who died that way.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: something whose outcome is undecided or risked is in question, while the martyr's death was literally at the post of execution.

clue.text: Untrustworthy sort is taking head off fish

indicators.note: a head is the top or front of something, so removing it drops the opening letter

blocks.note: a heel is a cad, someone who lets others down

explanation.surface: A shady character is busy beheading fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The heel and his 's join first to make HEELS, and only then is the head taken off. 'Fish' is plural here, which is why the answer ends in S.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: these snakelike creatures are one kind of fish, and 'fish' works as a plural to match.

clue.text: Stays and strap holding old woman securely at first

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within your grasp, so one piece sits inside another
only what comes first is wanted, so just the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: a rein is a strap for controlling a horse
one's old woman can be one's mother, MA

explanation.surface: Corset stays and a strap that hold an old woman in securely: a description of Victorian underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stays' looks like a noun, the stiffening in a corset, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean continuing to be in the same place or condition.

clue.text: As papal succession, so topical after Reformation

indicators.note: read as re-formation, the letters are formed again into a new order

explanation.surface: The line of popes became a hot topic after the Reformation.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital R makes it the Reformation that split the church from Rome, but read as re-formation it tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the claimed unbroken line of bishops, popes included, descending from Christ's twelve disciples.

clue.text: Tree feller going round copse in the middle

indicators.note: only the central part is wanted, so just the centre letter of the word is kept
going round something means encircling it, so one piece surrounds the other

explanation.surface: A lumberjack, a tree feller, walks round the middle of a copse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tree feller' reads as a woodcutter, but 'Tree' is the definition and 'feller' is informal for a fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the source of syrup, whose leaf is on Canada's flag, is one kind of tree.

clue.text: Determination comes after second drink

indicators.note: read literally as word order, this puts the piece before it behind the one that follows

explanation.surface: Resolve kicks in only after the second drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second drink' reads as one round too many, but 'second' only gives S and 'drink' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with colour: the verb means gulping large quantities greedily, as pigs do with their slops.

clue.text: French said to be holding back army unit in desert as before

definitions.note: 'as before' marks the old sense: demerit once meant desert, what one deserves

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters run right to left
to hold something is to keep it within your grasp, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: REME, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers of the British Army

explanation.surface: A French report that a unit is retreating across the desert, just as it did before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' is not sand but a noun from 'deserve', as in just deserts; in older English a demerit was simply a desert, good or bad.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic sense: the word formerly meant worth or what one has earned, before it narrowed to a fault.

clue.text: Permit Oslo or Rome to slip badly as big city

indicators.note: something done badly is botched and disordered, so the letters come out in a jumbled order

blocks.note: a second set of fodder with exactly the same ten letters, offered as an alternative

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to let Oslo or Rome decline badly as a big city.
explanation.walkthrough: A rare double anagram: PERMIT OSLO and ROME TO SLIP use the same ten letters, and either jumbled gives the answer; 'or' offers the choice.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: from the Greek for 'mother city', the word now means any large, busy urban centre or capital.

clue.text: Cleaner with a disqualification caught coach

explanation.surface: A cleaner is banned, and a sports coach is caught up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a trainer, but it is the vehicle; a char is a British cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an old-fashioned open motor bus with bench seats, used for day trips and outings.

clue.text: St John’s view as he converted sectarian

indicators.note: to convert something is to change its form, so the letters are turned into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: The apostle's outlook as he won a sectarian to his faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converted' fits the religious surface perfectly, which hides its anagram job.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sectarian is a member of a sect, and this Christian movement founded in 19th-century America is one.

clue.text: Boxer, one in Seoul getting whipped — short task to start with

indicators.note: something short is lacking its full length, so the word loses its final letter
whipping beats things up like eggs, so the letters are churned into a new order
this places the piece it follows at the very front of the answer

explanation.surface: A boxer in Seoul takes a beating after a brief job.
explanation.walkthrough: The I goes into SEOUL and the mix is jumbled; the task, minus its last letter, leads.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the American 'Brown Bomber' was world heavyweight champion from 1937 to 1949.

clue.text: Be sorry over bluish gas that all but covers continent

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over flips it so it reads upwards

blocks.note: to rue is to be sorry
ozone is a pale blue gas

explanation.surface: A lament over the blue haze of gas blanketing most of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive: the currency bloc spreads over most, but not all, of the continent.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the group of countries sharing the euro currency spans most of mainland Europe but not all of it.

clue.text: Salesman halving capital returned to become top man

indicators.note: to halve something is to split it into two parts, leaving a gap where another piece can be inserted
something returned is sent back where it came from, so the whole reads the other way

blocks.note: the Italian capital, split into its halves
a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: A salesman who split the capital comes back to be the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: RO-REP-ME read backwards gives EMPEROR, fittingly the top man of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose description rather than a synonym: the ruler of an empire outranks kings, so being the highest male figure fits.

clue.text: Prize tree getting this fertiliser

blocks.note: a pot is a trophy cup, a prize

explanation.surface: A prize-winning tree has been fed this fertiliser.
explanation.walkthrough: A pot is the cup handed out as a trophy, hence prize; 'this' points the wordplay at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this potassium compound is a common garden feed for flowers and fruit.

clue.text: Victorian craftsman releasing mass preparation for perfumier

indicators.note: to release something is to let it go, so that letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: William Morris, Victorian designer and craftsman
M = mass, the physics symbol, which is removed

explanation.surface: A Victorian craftsman gives up a mass of stock to make a perfume.
explanation.walkthrough: William Morris was the Arts and Crafts designer famous for wallpapers and textiles.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the powdered root of an iris is used in perfumery as a fixative.

clue.text: Slender student beastly doctor admits in south-east

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them inside, so one piece takes in another
being in something means sitting inside it, so the combined pair goes within a third piece

blocks.note: a doctor for beasts, a vet

explanation.surface: A slim student is admitted to a horrible doctor's surgery in the south-east of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' reads as nasty, but it means 'of beasts'; L for student comes from the L-plates on British learner drivers' cars.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from French, adding a hint of gracefulness to plain thinness.

clue.text: Maidservant, perhaps middle-class, raised son to Noah

indicators.note: only the middle part is wanted, so just the central letter of the following word is kept
in a down clue, raising something lifts it so it reads upwards

blocks.note: Ham was one of Noah's three sons

explanation.surface: A middle-class maid brings up a son for Noah.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle-class' looks like one social word, but it splits to give the middle letter of 'class'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a nursemaid or domestic servant in East or South Asia; 'perhaps' because not every maidservant is one.

clue.text: Playful animal caddish chap decapitated

indicators.note: to be decapitated is to lose one's head, so the word gives up its opening letter

blocks.note: a rotter is old British slang for a cad, a man who behaves badly

explanation.surface: Some animal is cast as a bounder who comes to a grisly end, losing his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotter is dated British slang for a scoundrel; once its R goes, the playful animal is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this river creature is famous for frolicking, sliding down mud banks and juggling pebbles.

clue.text: In French street Liberal appears to wield power

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician on a Paris street seems set to take power.
explanation.walkthrough: A rue is a street in a French town, as in the Rue de Rivoli in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a verb for governing a country or people, matching the verb phrase in the clue.

clue.text: For dictator maybe canes will do!

indicators.note: someone dictating speaks the words, so the letters come from how they sound

blocks.note: canes are bamboos, and 'will' contracts to 'll

explanation.surface: A tyrant, it seems, will make do with a caning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' looks like a tyrant who might use canes, but here it is someone dictating to a secretary; 'do' is the slang for cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British sense: 'do' can mean cheat or con, as in 'I've been done', and the answer means trick too.

clue.text: Hormone damage when temperature dropped at home

indicators.note: something dropped is let fall and left behind, so that letter is removed from the word

blocks.note: an insult in medicine is an injury or damage to the body

explanation.surface: A hormone does harm once the heating is turned down at home.
explanation.walkthrough: An insult in medical language is damage to the body, as in 'a brain insult'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the pancreas produces this chemical messenger to regulate blood sugar.

clue.text: Overhead protection in the rain collapsed

indicators.note: something collapsed has fallen apart, so its letters are rebuilt in a different order

explanation.surface: An umbrella gave way in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an umbrella; the answer is a fine mesh worn over the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic-leaning description: the mesh sits on top of the head and keeps hair in place, literally guarding from above.
